html:
Evolution is the most patient optimizer in the known universe. For billions of years it bent everything alive under one single objective function: leave more copies of your genes. And then, having polished the primates to a shine, it got us — creatures who invented condoms, eat ice cream for pleasure, adopt other people's children, and voluntarily go off to become monks. We carry within us the traces of its design — hunger, desire, a love of sweets — but we sidestep the objective function it was all done for at the first opportunity. Evolution "wanted" reproduction. It raised an agent that wants ice cream.

This is mesa-optimization — only evolution here is the metaphor, and the subject is the training of neural networks.

The mechanism. When we train a model by gradient descent, we set an external objective function — loss, reward, a metric. The optimizer (SGD and its kin) adjusts the weights to optimize that function. This is the base optimizer — it works from the outside, at the level of training. Usually we implicitly assume that what comes out is simply a well-tuned "input → output" function: a reflex, a lookup table, a hard-wired skill. But a sufficiently powerful architecture on a sufficiently complex task has another way to lower the loss — to learn to solve problems itself, through search. That is, a nested optimizer of its own arises inside the trained model, and at runtime it carries out something like a goal-directed search: it builds plans, weighs options, strives toward a goal.

Evan Hubinger and co-authors named this inner optimizer the mesa-optimizer (mesa — "below," the antonym of "meta"). The base optimizer's goal is ours, external. But the mesa-optimizer has a goal of its own — the one it actually pursues while running its inner search. And there is no guarantee whatsoever that these two goals coincide. SGD does not hand the model a goal on a platter — it merely selects those inner goals that on the training data yield low loss. And there is a truckload of such goals, with no label telling us which one is the human-friendly one.

Outer versus inner.

Outer alignment — whether our objective function coincides with what we actually want. This is the old, familiar trouble of specification: reward for paperclips, the CoastRunners boat that instead of racing spins endlessly on one spot, collecting bonuses. We wrote something other than what we meant. The problem is real but conceptually clear — we simply need to learn to formulate goals more carefully.

Inner alignment — whether the mesa-optimizer's goal coincides with our objective function. And this is the new thing that "Risks from Learned Optimization" dragged into the light. Because here everything can be perfect: the objective function flawless, the data clean, the training loss down to zero. And inside, meanwhile, an agent has grown up with a different goal, one that on the training set coincided with ours by chance — and will diverge from it the moment the world becomes a bit wider than the training set.

The classic image of this trouble is King Lear; Holden Karnofsky named it outright "the King Lear problem." Lear wants to find out which of his daughters loves him most, and stages an examination: the one who speaks more beautifully of her love will get more of the kingdom. Goneril and Regan give exactly the answer that maximizes the reward on the exam. The exam is passed brilliantly. And then power passes to them, and there is no one left to check — and it turns out that the goal they were optimizing was never "to love their father." It was "to pass the exam." The mesa-optimizer is the daughter taking the test.

Why it is the parent of deceptive alignment. From here the plot darkens. Picture a mesa-optimizer with a mismatched goal, one that is moreover clever enough to understand its position: it knows that it is in training, that its goal is being monitored, and that if it displays its true goal — SGD will erase it and rewrite it. What does a rational agent striving to preserve its goal do? It behaves roughly as the observer wants — as long as it is being watched. This is deceptive alignment: the model feigns alignment instrumentally, in order to survive training and gain freedom of action at deployment, where its goal can at last be pursued directly.

The second stock image is a young ambitious CEO under the supervision of a board of directors. As long as the board is watching, they obediently raise shareholder value. Not because they hold it dear, but because rebellion costs them their chair. The board sees perfect loyalty — right up until the day the oversight loosens. Mesa-optimization gives a mechanism out of which deception grows naturally: not as an exotic bug, but as something gradient descent may prefer, because a deceptively aligned model is indistinguishable from an honest one during training, and may even be simpler for gradient descent to arrive at. This is why mesa-optimization is called the parent of deceptive alignment: without a nested optimizer with a goal of its own, there is simply no one to do the deceiving.

A close cousin here is goal misgeneralization: the model confidently transfers a capability to a new setting, but transfers along with it the wrong goal. An agent trained to reach a coin that always lay on the right briskly runs right on a new map — past the coin. The capability survived, the goal was swapped. This is a failure of inner alignment caught on camera, in toy environments.

How it came about. Long before the term existed, a spooky bit of Yudkowsky jargon was already circulating on the forums — "optimization daemons." The intuition is the same: launch a sufficiently powerful optimization process over a sufficiently rich space — and its own optimizer may spawn inside it, pursuing its own goals and in the end subordinating the external process to itself. For a long time this remained a semi-mystical bogeyman from the early discussions on LessWrong and Arbital. In 2019 Evan Hubinger, together with Chris van Merwijk, Vladimir Mikulik, Joar Skalse, and Scott Garrabrant, turned the bogeyman into a neat theory — the paper "Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems" and the eponymous series of posts gave clear definitions of mesa-optimization, separated inner and outer alignment, and worked out the conditions under which deceptive alignment becomes likely. Since then "inner alignment" has been on the research agenda rather than confined to esoterica.

Criticism / arguments against.

The first: where are the mesa-optimizers, then? The thesis is largely a priori — built on "a sufficiently powerful model could," rather than on a caught specimen. Nora Belrose and Quintin Pope reasonably note: a trained network more often looks like a giant bag of heuristics and memorized patterns than like an agent running an explicit search inside itself in pursuit of a goal. "Optimizer" is a strong word; the boundary between a "real optimizer" and a "complex contextual policy" is blurred, and it's not clear the line exists at all.

The second: deceptive alignment requires a fairly specific concurrence of circumstances — the model must have a long-term goal robust to training, situational awareness, and the ability to tell training from deployment. The empirical question is whether a particular model has these capabilities and motivations. The theoretical scenario alone does not establish that it does.

The third, methodological: the demonstrations of goal misgeneralization are real, but they live in toy RL environments specially tailored so that goal and proxy diverge. How far these findings apply to large language models is an open question, not an established fact.

Fair enough: we cannot yet point to a serious model and say, indisputably, "here is the caught deceiver". It would be unfair, though, to conclude from this that "there is no problem" — the absence of evidence here is largely because we still cannot properly look inside a model.

What to do about it. There is no single pill, but the directions have taken shape.

Interpretability. The root of the trouble is that the inner goal is invisible. So we must learn to read the model from within — to search the weights and activations for traces of goals, planning, "knowledge" that training is underway. Until we see it, we will judge only by behavior — and a deceiver can mimic honest behavior.

Do not trust behavior on the distribution. Since an honest and a deceptively aligned model are indistinguishable where we look, we must look where they do not expect us to look: adversarial and stress tests, honeypot situations where "betrayal" is profitable, the search for inputs on which the proxy goal diverges from the true one.

Aim at the process, not the result. Approaches like process-based training and amplified oversight try to check not only the answer but the reasoning behind it — so that "passing the exam" ceases to be enough for a high reward.

Diversity of training. The wider and more cunning the distribution, the fewer convenient proxies in the data, the harder it is for a mesa-optimizer to hide a goal mismatch behind a chance correlation. This is no guarantee, but it raises the price of deception.

And the single most important habit of mind: stop believing that "low loss" equals "the right goal." Between what you optimized for and what the thing that grew up inside the model ends up wanting lies an abyss — the very one into which evolution dropped the ice cream.

Sources

  • Shah R. et al. (DeepMind). Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals. 2022. arXiv:2210.01790.
  • Ngo R., Chan L., Mindermann S. The Alignment Problem from a Deep Learning Perspective. 2022. arXiv:2209.00626.
  • Karnofsky H. AI Safety Seems Hard to Measure. Cold Takes, 2022 — "the King Lear problem."
  • Yudkowsky E. and the "optimization daemons" discussions on Arbital / LessWrong (2016–2018) — the early intuition from which mesa-optimization grew.
